matter_reference_date_basis: exam_session OCTOBER 2023 in candidates/matters/M038.json; the law is taken as it stood at that session.
corpus_gaps: The rate of stamp duty prescribed under s.37 of the Financial Statute of the Western Province No. 06 of 1990 is not in the corpus. The Statute charges duty at the prescribed rate and the prescribing Order was never extracted, so the rupee amount cannot be computed.

No Order under s.76(1) or regulation under s.77 of the Financial Statute is in the corpus, so the prescribed bank, the prescribed forms and the prescribed stamp descriptions referred to in ss.40 and 62 cannot be identified.

The corpus text of s.106 of the Financial Statute has lost the quoted defined-term labels through OCR, so the definitions of Transfer, gift and value had to be matched to their terms using the section's defined_terms metadata rather than the body text.

The commencement Order under s.1 of the Financial Statute is not in the corpus. The corpus records in_force_from_year 1990, and s.78(5) refers to instruments stamped under the Statute from 1 January 1991, which is the only in-corpus indication of when Part 3 began to operate.

That Kadawatha lies in the Gampaha District of the Western Province is geography, not a corpus fact; no schedule of provincial or district boundaries is in the corpus, and the whole analysis depends on it.

Different rates may be prescribed in respect of different classes or categories of instruments.
provisions.why_relevant: Charging section. Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, at the prescribed rate. The land and house are at Kadawatha, in the Gampaha District of the Western Province, so the deed of gift falls within this charge. The section fixes no rate itself; the rate is prescribed by subsidiary legislation that is not in the corpus.

provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the base of the calculation: duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on the consideration (a gift has none) and not automatically on the current market price.

provisions.why_relevant: The operative valuation rule. For gifted immovable property acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977, value is the open market price at the date the donor acquired it, increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the gift. The donor acquired the land in February 1980, so paragraph (c) applies and not paragraph (b).

questions.authority_requirement_reason: Both limbs of the question, the amount of stamp duty and the procedure, are governed by statute. The charge, the valuation rule for gifted immovable property, the person liable, the time and mode of payment and the notary's certification duties are all in the Financial Statute of the Western Province No. 06 of 1990. No judicial authority or Roman-Dutch doctrine is needed. What is missing is not case law but subsidiary legislation: the Order prescribing the rate under section 37, which is not in the corpus.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a deed of gift of land and a house at Kadawatha is an instrument chargeable with stamp duty, and under which enactment.
On what amount the duty is calculated: the 1980 purchase price plus the cost of the house, or the present market value of Rs. 5,400,000.
What rate applies to that value and therefore what sum is payable.
Who must pay the duty, and by what procedure it is paid, evidenced and attested before and at execution.

questions.hop_count_basis: Four necessary linked steps: section 37 charges duty on an instrument transferring immovable property in the Western Province; the section 106 definition of Transfer brings a gift within that charge; section 48(1) directs that duty be calculated on the value of the property conveyed; and the section 106 definition of value, paragraph (c) with its lower-of limb, fixes that value for immovable property gifted by a donor who acquired it after March 31, 1977. The payment provisions (sections 51 and 40) are a parallel required step for the procedure limb of the question, not a fifth hop.

enrichment.original_background: In 1980 February Dayani Perera had purchased a land in extent of 15 perches situated in Kadawatha for Rs. 400,000/- and constructed a house on it. The cost of construction of the house was Rs. 3,100,000/-. She wishes to gift this house and land to her son Saranga and she instructs you to prepare a Deed of Gift. The present market value of the house and property is Rs. 5,400,000/-.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the proposed deed of gift of the Kadawatha land and house from Dayani Perera to her son Saranga is chargeable with stamp duty, on what amount that duty is calculated, at what rate, by whom it is payable and by what procedure it must be paid and attested.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The land is at Kadawatha, in the Gampaha District of the Western Province, so stamp duty on an instrument transferring it is a provincial charge under the Financial Statute of the Western Province No. 06 of 1990. Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.13 leaves instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property outside that Act's scheme. Financial Statute s.37 charges duty at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, and s.106 defines Transfer to include a gift, a gift itself being a voluntary transfer without consideration in money or money's worth. No exemption in s.39 covers a gift between private persons. By s.48(1) the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed. Where the property gifted is immovable property acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977, s.106 defines value as the open market price at the date the donor acquired it increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the gift, or the open market price at the date of the deed of gift, whichever is the lower. The rate to be applied to that value is not fixed by the Statute; s.37 leaves it to be prescribed. Duty is payable by the grantee under s.51(a) unless the parties agree otherwise. Under s.40(1) it must be paid before or at the time of execution and shown on the instrument by adhesive or impressed stamps or a certificate of payment; under s.40(2) duty on an instrument transferring immovable property may be paid to a prescribed bank, which issues a certificate of payment to be affixed to the instrument. The attesting notary must under s.78(2) to (4) satisfy himself that the value on which duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed, affix, cancel and recite any adhesive stamps in the attestation, and where payment was made to a bank certify that the bank's certificate has been duly affixed to the duplicate. If the value is doubtful the instrument, executed or not, may be taken to an Assessor for adjudication under s.62 on payment of the prescribed fee.
gold_answer_draft.application: Dayani Perera acquired the 15 perches at Kadawatha in February 1980, that is after March 31, 1977, so paragraph (c) of the s.106 definition of value applies and not paragraph (b). The first figure is the open market price at acquisition, Rs. 400,000, increased by the cost of the improvement made afterwards, the house built at a cost of Rs. 3,100,000, giving Rs. 3,500,000. The second figure is the open market price at the date of the deed of gift, Rs. 5,400,000. The lower of the two is Rs. 3,500,000, so that is the value on which duty is chargeable under s.48(1) and the present market value of Rs. 5,400,000 is not the base. The rate to be applied to Rs. 3,500,000 is the rate prescribed under s.37; that Order is not in the frozen corpus, so the arithmetic cannot be completed from the sources available and the money figure is left open. On procedure, Saranga as grantee is the person liable under s.51(a) unless the deed provides otherwise; the duty must be paid before or at execution, in practice to a prescribed bank under s.40(2) with the bank's certificate affixed to the deed; and the notary preparing the deed must set out in it the facts affecting chargeability, satisfy himself as to the value and give the s.78(4) certification in the attestation. Because value here rests on the Assessor's opinion of two open market prices and on proof of the Rs. 3,100,000 spent on construction, adjudication under s.62 before execution is the safe course.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The deed of gift is chargeable with provincial stamp duty under s.37 of the Financial Statute of the Western Province No. 06 of 1990, computed on a value of Rs. 3,500,000, being Rs. 400,000 acquisition price plus Rs. 3,100,000 cost of construction, that total being lower than the Rs. 5,400,000 present market value. It is payable by the donee Saranga before or at the time of execution, normally to a prescribed bank with the certificate of payment affixed to the deed and certified by the attesting notary. The rupee amount of the duty cannot be stated from the corpus, because the Order prescribing the rate under s.37 is not among the available sources; the question is left blocked on that point rather than answered with a rate taken from outside the corpus.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty on an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province is charged at the prescribed rate by section 37 of the Financial Statute of the Western Province No. 06 of 1990.

Stamp duty on transfers of immovable property was not brought within the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006, which expressly excludes such instruments from the displacement of the earlier stamp duty law.

Transfer in the Financial Statute includes a gift, so a deed of gift of land is an instrument relating to a transfer for the purposes of section 37; a gift is a voluntary transfer without consideration in money or money's worth.
None of the exemptions in section 39 covers a gift of land between private individuals.
Where property is conveyed by an instrument the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed.

For immovable property gifted by a donor who acquired it after March 31, 1977, value means the open market price at the date of acquisition increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made before the gift, or the open market price at the date of the deed of gift, whichever is the lower.

Because the donor acquired the Kadawatha land in February 1980, paragraph (c) of the definition of value applies rather than paragraph (b), which is confined to property acquired on or before March 31, 1977.
The acquisition-plus-improvements figure is Rs. 400,000 plus Rs. 3,100,000, that is Rs. 3,500,000.
Rs. 3,500,000 is lower than the Rs. 5,400,000 open market value at the date of the gift, so the chargeable value is Rs. 3,500,000 and not the present market value.
The duty on the deed of gift is payable by the donee Saranga as grantee, unless the deed provides otherwise.

The duty must be paid before or at the time of execution and evidenced on the deed by stamps or a certificate of payment; for a transfer of immovable property it may be paid to a prescribed bank, which issues the certificate to be affixed to the instrument.

The attesting notary must satisfy himself that the value on which duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed, deal with and recite any adhesive stamps, and where payment was made to a bank certify that the bank's certificate of payment has been affixed to the duplicate.

Because the chargeable value depends on the Assessor's opinion of open market prices, the deed may be submitted for adjudication to an Assessor on payment of the prescribed fee for a written determination of the duty chargeable.
The deed of gift is chargeable with stamp duty computed on a value of Rs. 3,500,000, payable by Saranga before or at the time of execution.
The rupee amount of the duty cannot be stated from the corpus, because section 37 leaves the rate to be prescribed and the prescribing Order is not among the corpus sources.

questions.block_reason: The question demands a calculated figure and a shown method. The method is fully supported by the corpus and yields a chargeable value of Rs. 3,500,000, but section 37 of the Financial Statute fixes no rate: it charges duty at the prescribed rate, and the Order prescribing the rate for transfers of immovable property in the Western Province is not in the frozen corpus. The final rupee amount therefore cannot be derived from any provision in the corpus and has not been supplied from memory.
